paras: The Florence election riot was an attack on Black voters at the polls at or near Florence, South Carolina, on election day, November 7, 1882, in which two or three "colored men" were shot and the election there was broken up. The news came chiefly from a telegram by E. H. Deas, the Republican candidate for Congress in the Sixth District, who said the men were shot for insisting on voting the Republican ticket. Wire reports turned his account into two or three killed, and Republican papers in the North cited it as an example of Democratic intimidation.

The 1882 congressional election in South Carolina pitted Democrats against Republicans, Greenbackers and Independents, and in the Sixth District Deas ran against the Democrat Dargan. A Columbia dispatch to the New-York Tribune reported "serious disturbances" across the state that day, with armed "red shirts" capturing polls and driving off Black and Independent voters in several counties.

According to Deas, a riot broke out at Florence "about noon" on November 7, though the Associated Press version placed it in the morning. In the fullest text of his telegram he wrote that three colored men were "fatally shot because they insist on voting the Republican ticket" and that Democrats were trying "to intimidate all the negroes possible." He named Frank Gray and Samuel Evans as the two who were fatally shot and said both were afterward arrested and placed in the guard-house. The election, he said, was broken up, and the Tribune's Columbia correspondent likewise reported that several colored men were shot at the Florence polls and that Republican and Independent voting stopped at noon.
A Washington special added that a "democratic mob, in red shirts" had raided the election booths and killed three negroes, after which the polls were closed for the day.

On November 8 Deas told the Republican Congressional Committee that he had been defeated "by the usual Democratic methods in preventing voters from attending the polls." No report in the coverage confirms whether Gray, Evans or a third man died, and no arrest of the attackers, inquest or prosecution appears.

The story reached most papers as a one-sentence Associated Press item, printed among election returns or crime news on November 8 from Memphis and St. Paul to Omaha and Sacramento. The wire garbled Deas's name as "S. H. Dears," "A. H. Dean" or "A. V. Deas" and his district as the Second, and a Western Associated Press version in the Las Vegas Daily Gazette ran under the head "A Riot in North Carolina." The St. Paul Daily Globe headed the item "TWO DARKIES KILLED," while weeklies in Ohio and Minnesota still repeated it a week later.

Republican papers gave it a partisan frame: the Portland Daily Press ran the red-shirt version as "INTIMIDATED," and the New-York Tribune grouped Florence under "THE POLLS CAPTURED BY RED-SHIRTS." Washington's Evening Critic printed Deas's full telegram on election evening, and the National Republican set it beside Charleston and Columbia dispatches calling the vote "the most quiet and peaceful election" in South Carolina for many years.

The number of dead differed by version: the Associated Press said two colored men were killed and several wounded, the Washington special and the Springfield Weekly Republican said three negroes were killed, and Deas's own telegram spoke of men fatally shot of whom "two or three" would die. Since every count traces to Deas's same-day telegram, the wire's word "killed" may have run ahead of the source. Democratic dispatches from Columbia, which did not mention Florence, said the election passed off quietly across the state and that both parties polled a fair vote in Darlington.

reader.title: Florence election riot (1882)
bases: Reports describe Democratic partisans, called a mob in red shirts, attacking Black voters at the Florence polls, shooting two or three and breaking up the election, an attack on Black voters as a group rather than on one accused person (A2, A3, A13).

Deas's telegram (A2, A4, A6) and a separate Columbia dispatch to the New-York Tribune (A13) agree that colored men were shot at the Florence polls and opposition voting stopped; Democratic dispatches calling the state election quiet (A6) do not mention Florence.
